<h3 class="wp-block-heading"><strong>Build an AI platform that survives production</strong></h3>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Move beyond the demo. Compare open approaches to GPU scheduling and utilization, model serving, inference routing, AI gateways, networking, storage, observability, security, and agent infrastructure—with the people building and operating the technologies.</p>



<p class="wp-block-paragraph">With an <a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/register/">All-Access pass</a>, start Monday at Cloud Native AI + Inference Day or Agentics Day, then continue through three days of AI, platform engineering, operations, observability, security, and maintainer sessions.</p>

							<section class="sz-speaker-detail" data-speaker-id="54570209-5ec9-4392-9680-38679ee15e97">
					<h3>Michael Amundson</h3>

											<p class="sz-speaker-detail__title">Distinguished Engineer</p>
					
											<p class="sz-speaker-detail__company">CVS Health</p>
					
											<p class="sz-speaker-detail__bio">Michael Amundson is a distinguished engineer in the Developer Experience organization at CVS Health where he leads technical direction for the CAP Application Platform. His near decade of experience in platform engineering started at Target Corporation, where he helped build Target's in-house application platform. Prior to his work on platforms, Michael worked as an application engineer in roles across a number of Fortune 500 companies, daydreaming of platforms that didn't yet exist.</p>
					
											<ul class="sz-speaker-detail__links">
															<li>
									<a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/michaelamundson" rel="noopener nofollow" target="_blank">LinkedIn</a>
								</li>
															<li>
									<a href="https://www.cvshealth.com/" rel="noopener nofollow" target="_blank">Company Website</a>
								</li>
													</ul>
					
											<h4>Conference Sessions</h4>
						<ul class="sz-speaker-detail__sessions">
																							<li>
									<a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/program/schedule/?id=1302691">
										Beyond End User: CAP and the Evolution of Open Source at CVS Health									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 11, 2026 • 10:23 AM-10:28 AM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Two years ago, the DevEx organization at CVS Health set an audacious plan in motion: build a platform capable of running the company’s thousands of existing applications while remaining approachable enough that someone joining the company could ship a new application on their very first day. To make this work, we knew we would need to leverage many of the incredible open source projects across the CNCF landscape. But we also knew that achieving our goal would require software we’d have to build: a meta control plane that could weave these projects together into a single streamlined platform. We call the platform CAP and we’re excited to share its design, show a brief demo, and talk about our transition from end user to open source maintainer and contributor as CAP evolves from an internal platform to a brand new open source project.</p>
																	</li>
													</ul>
									</section>

											<p class="sz-speaker-detail__company">Google</p>
					
											<p class="sz-speaker-detail__bio">Sunil Arora is a software engineer on the GKE team at Google Cloud and a long-time Kubernetes contributor. He was an original author and lead maintainer of Kubebuilder, has made foundational contributions to kubectl, kustomize, and kpt, and co-authored kubectl-ai. He now leads OpenRL, Kubernetes-native post-training infrastructure for LLMs. For over a decade, Sunil has built tools that help developers and platform teams safely deploy and manage applications at scale.</p>

											<h4>Conference Sessions</h4>
						<ul class="sz-speaker-detail__sessions">
																							<li>
									<a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/program/schedule/?id=1349401">
										Pods in the Wild: Reinforcement Learning on Kubernetes with OpenRL									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 10, 2026 • 9:32 AM-9:40 AM</span>

																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">What do wild dolphins, open-weight Gemma models, and Kubernetes have in common?
Pods, of course!
By training DolphinGemma on decades of marine acoustic data, researchers are actively decoding dolphin communication. This reflects a broader industry shift: transformative AI pairs domain-specific open weights with specialized data. Far from replacing frontier models, winning architectures unite massive foundation LLMs for broad reasoning with lightweight, task-tuned models for targeted execution. While frontier models set the bar for general intelligence, the next major operational leap belongs to everyday builders: empowering practitioners to fine-tune open-weight models that outperform massive frontier baselines on domain-specific tasks at a fraction of the cost, footprint, and latency.
Historically, reinforcement learning (RL) was trapped inside elite research labs and brittle, complex runtimes. A new CNCF sandbox project, OpenRL fundamentally changes this paradigm by democratizing RL directly on Kubernetes. Now, a builder can articulate a task, point to a dataset, and use CNCF technologies to guide an open-weight model toward task mastery without requiring deep machine learning expertise.</p>

													</ul>

						<ul class="sz-speaker-detail__sessions">
																							<li>
									<a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/program/schedule/?id=1334821">
										Integrating Envoy AI Gateway and Kyverno Authz for Realtime Governance of LLM and MCP Traffic									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 10, 2026 • 4:30 PM-4:55 PM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Solutions Showcase | Halls 5 | Cosmic Canyon Zone</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Agentic AI has evolved models from passive text generators into active operators that invoke APIs, query databases, and execute tool calls. Standard Kubernetes RBAC cannot govern non-deterministic actions driven by unvalidated prompts. This session presents a cloud-native architecture that integrates the Envoy AI Gateway with Kyverno’s declarative policy model to govern autonomous AI intent before execution. The session demonstrates how Envoy acts as a specialized data plane for LLM traffic, using Envoy’s External Processing API to "de-frame" Model Context Protocol (MCP) payloads. The Kyverno service then intercepts these extracted intents, applying declarative, YAML-based policies to authorize or block model actions in real time. Attendees will explore techniques to inspect MCP payloads at the gateway layer, author policy rules for AI agents, and enforce zero-trust boundaries without altering underlying agent code.</p>
																	</li>
																							<li>
									<a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/program/schedule/?id=1250559">
										GitOps Meltdown: How a Commit Triggered a Cascading Delete of 39 Clusters in Production									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 10, 2026 • 5:30 PM-6:00 PM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 BC</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">GitOps assumes cluster state converges to Git.But, what happens when the desired state is wrong?
This session examines a real incident where a routine Flux reconciliation turned a small git change into a cascading prune across a Kubernetes management platform managing 39 workload clusters. A missing Kustomization triggered inventory deletion, causing Flux controller to delete itself during reconciliation. Resulting in orphaned resources, stuck finalizers, and loss of critical Git repository storage.
Using timelines and incident evidence, we trace the failure chain and explore Flux inventory tracking, pruning, finalizers, StatefulSet PVC ownership, CSI reclaim policies, and deletion ordering.
We also cover recovery, restoring resources, rebuilding the GitOps control plane, and safely resuming reconciliation. Attendees will learn practical ways to reduce GitOps blast radius, protect stateful infrastructure, and build platforms that remain recoverable when automation fails.</p>
																	</li>
																							<li>
									<a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/program/schedule/?id=1293929">
										Standardized Yet Adaptable: How Nutanix is Evolving Cluster API with CAREN									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 12, 2026 • 9:39 AM-9:44 AM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Cloud native innovation has always been driven by the community. From Mesosphere's role as a CNCF founding member to D2iQ's continued Kubernetes leadership and now Nutanix's active contributions across multiple CNCF projects, the mission has remained the same: build together in the open.In this session, we'll revisit that journey and explore how those experiences led to CAREN (Cluster API Runtime Extensions – Nutanix), an extensible framework that enables dynamic cluster configuration and lifecycle management while preserving the simplicity and consistency of Cluster API's declarative model. As we look to the future of Kubernetes fleet management, standardization via Cluster API (CAPI) and the ClusterClass feature has brought immense consistency to cluster provisioning. However, real-world enterprise deployments often hit a wall: they require dynamic customization that strict standardization struggles to accommodate.CAREN bridges the critical gap between strict declarative blueprints and real-world adaptability. By leveraging CAPI's runtime mutation hooks, CAREN dynamically configures and manages Kubernetes clusters without ever needing to fork or touch the base ClusterClass. It empowers platform engineering teams to deliver standardized, yet infinitely adaptable Kubernetes clusters.</p>
																	</li>
													</ul>

																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Agents and agent-like workloads are becoming a predominant class of workloads on Kubernetes, but they are different from "traditional" apps. 										We Have GitOps at Home: How Meta Went from Terraform on Cron to GitOps for AI Infra									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 11, 2026 • 9:57 AM-10:02 AM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">At Meta, ~15 engineers run ~100 Kubernetes clusters for AI research & inference. Terraform exceeds expectations at its job: setting up infra for those clusters. The problem is its side gig: deploying the k8s apps. Even a one-line Helm values change can take a working day in our monolithic Terraform pipeline, where one stuck app can block dozens of others.
In the new model, Terraform didn't get fired, just reorged. Kargo and Argo CD take over the apps, so each app ships on its own and a routine update is live and healthy in minutes.
Terraform's side gig now comes down to installing ArgoCD. That's the easy part. The hard part is making GitOps work with Meta's internal systems: one-way config syncs from our in-house VCS to Git, an app "order form" instead of hand-written YAMLs, and multi-tenant ArgoCD(s) instead of one per cluster.
If your company also runs on many homegrown systems, our lessons can save you a few headaches.</p>

																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Just as the Linux ecosystem thrives by separating a universal, low-level kernel from specialized distributions, Kubernetes is evolving beyond a monolithic, "one-size-fits-all" architecture. To solve this, the industry is implicitly defining a lean Kubernetes Kernel—the core API machinery, reconciliation loops, and resource abstractions—as a standardized foundation. Simultaneously, agentic engineering is drastically reducing the cost of software creation and democratizing the operational expertise needed to build upon this foundation.
Join us to learn how building on the Kubernetes Kernel allows power-users to create vertically integrated, purpose-built custom distros that achieve significant performance gains while still crowd-sourcing defect discovery and reliability.</p>

																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Cloud native teams spent a decade building traffic infrastructure they control: open source, decentralized, observable, and running on Kubernetes. 																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Kubernetes disruption handling is evolving from a collection of custom solutions and workarounds into a more cooperative lifecycle model. 																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Grand Ballroom ACE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Distributed AI training fails fast: if a single GPU pod in a multi-node job cannot schedule, accelerators sit idle or the workload fails with collective-op timeouts. To compensate, the ecosystem evolved many external schedulers, including Kueue, Volcano, and KAI, each forcing controllers to pick a side.
Kubernetes 1.36 changes this. The new Workload and PodGroup APIs (KEP-4671) introduce scheduler-native primitives for gang-scheduling, topology-aware placement, and coordinated use of high-bandwidth interconnects such as IMEX. TrainJob, JobSet, and LeaderWorkerSet are converging on these APIs.
This session covers Kubeflow Trainer’s adoption (KEP-3015): why TrainJob owns Workload composition and how its plugin architecture enables advanced scheduling features. Attendees will see a demo of multi-node fine-tuning on modern accelerators, how the Workload API unifies a fragmented ecosystem, and how to adopt it in their own controllers.</p>

																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Since 2017, Kubeflow has evolved from a TensorFlow controller into a Cloud Native AI platform comprising eleven full-fledged projects, used by thousands of organizations across the AI lifecycle. This keynote explores real-world stories from our users, showing how an open, vendor-neutral community is pushing the boundaries of Data & AI infrastructure across the whole AI lifecycle. It will highlight large-scale distributed training with Kubeflow Trainer and MPI, and look ahead to the agentic era with innovations such as the Semantic Operator. By bringing governed semantic APIs to Kubernetes, the Semantic Operator enables AI agents, applications, and BI tools to work with trusted business definitions without relying on LLM-generated SQL. Together, these efforts illustrate how the Kubeflow community is building the foundations for the next decade of Cloud Native AI.</p>

										Agent Substrate: Open Layers for Agentic Systems									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 10, 2026 • 10:03 AM-10:10 AM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Running agentic workloads on Kubernetes presents several challenges. Agent Substrate is a new project, built on and with Kubernetes, which enables you to securely run huge numbers of agents on Kubernetes with ultra low latency.</p>
																	</li>
																							<li>
									<a href="https://events.linuxfoundation.org/kubecon-cloudnativecon-north-america/program/schedule/?id=1247753">
										Lessons Learned Sandboxing Agents with kagent									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 10, 2026 • 5:30 PM-6:00 PM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Is an agent a normal Kubernetes workload?
It needs compute, identity, networking, storage, and lifecycle management – so it looks like one. But an agent session is long-lived, stateful, bursty, and mostly idle.
And it can do anything a user can. That's what makes sandboxing critical.
The sandbox defines what the agent can see, touch, call, and persist: filesystem access, tool permissions, credentials, network policy, identity, and cleanup. Getting that boundary wrong is a security incident waiting to happen.
This talk covers the lessons we learned designing and implementing agent sandboxing for kagent – including NVIDIA's OpenShell, Kubernetes' agent-sandbox, and Google's substrate support – and what teams need to think about before trusting agents with code execution, credentials, network access, and production data.</p>

																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 2 | 255 A</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Curious how kagent brings agentic AI to the cloud native ecosystem? Interested in contributing to kagent ? Want to explore the codebase and understand what powers the kagent framework? Join the kagent maintainers for a hands-on contributor session where you'll learn how the project is built and how you can become part of its growing open source community.
We'll walk through the architecture of kagent, explore how agents and MCP tools work together, show you how to set up a local development environment, explain the project's community and contribution workflow, and help you get started with your first contribution. Whether you're new to the project or looking to become a regular contributor, you'll leave with the knowledge and confidence to make your first PR to kagent.</p>

										The Storage Bottleneck AI Didn't See Coming: Inside StepFun’s Multimodal Production Stack									</a>
																			<span class="sz-speaker-detail__when">Nov 12, 2026 • 9:51 AM-9:54 AM</span>
																												<span class="sz-speaker-detail__room">Salt Palace | Level 1 | Hall DE</span>
																												<p class="sz-speaker-detail__abstract">Multimodal AI has outgrown the storage systems built for it. Training and inference now mix small-file storms, high-concurrency random reads, terabyte-scale checkpoints, and 100 GB+ model files across heterogeneous GPU clusters, private data centers, and public clouds. The hard part isn't any one workload. It means serving all of them through a single storage access layer that follows compute wherever it runs, whether on-prem or in any cloud. In this keynote, we'll show how StepFun made that move on Kubernetes, TiKV, and JuiceFS. Hardware-aware CSI mounts handle heterogeneous nodes, TiKV-backed metadata scales to more than 10,000 mounting hosts, point-get optimization speeds up relevant read-only operations by roughly 50%, and tuning both the metadata engine and readahead for Safetensors loads cuts read amplification by roughly 71%. We'll share how these improvements were merged upstream to turn production lessons into community gains.</p>

common?\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EPods, of course!\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EBy training DolphinGemma on decades of marine acoustic data, researchers are actively decoding dolphin communication. This reflects a broader industry shift: transformative AI pairs domain-specific open weights with specialized data. Far from replacing frontier models, winning architectures unite massive foundation LLMs for broad reasoning with lightweight, task-tuned models for targeted execution. While frontier models set the bar for general intelligence, the next major operational leap belongs to everyday builders: empowering practitioners to fine-tune open-weight models that outperform massive frontier baselines on domain-specific tasks at a fraction of the cost, footprint, and latency.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EHistorically, reinforcement learning (RL) was trapped inside elite research labs and brittle, complex runtimes. A new CNCF sandbox project, OpenRL fundamentally changes this paradigm by democratizing RL directly on Kubernetes. Now, a builder can articulate a task, point to a dataset, and use CNCF technologies to guide an open-weight model toward task mastery without requiring deep machine learning expertise.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T09:32:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T09:40:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["01baf53b-c05d-4a69-aff6-b2accebc9c51","e3175872-2944-4e2b-bd15-e5e53f335565"]},{"id":"1301696","title":"Engineering Kubernetes for the Next Era of Workloads","description":"\u003Cp\u003EAI changed what Kubernetes has to handle: container images in the tens of gigabytes, clusters approaching 100,000 nodes, and accelerators a device count can\u2019t describe. At AWS we hit those limits early, and when we do, we fix them upstream. This keynote covers three layers. In containerd, parallel layer unpack takes the long pole out of pulling large AI images. In the control plane, we removed lock contention in the API server watch cache and the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and fixed a scheduler hot path, all in Kubernetes 1.37. For accelerators, Dynamic Resource Allocation lets a pod ask for a GPU and network adapter on the same PCIe root, and Karpenter can now provision for it, even for nodes that don\u2019t exist yet.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T09:42:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T09:47:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["d96c413a-8318-4289-a250-06d98504be45"]},{"id":"1363682","title":"Building the Next Generation of AI with Open Source","description":"\u003Cp\u003EJoin us to hear how NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source and working alongside the Kubernetes community to build the future of AI Factories\u2014together. The hard part is the move: bringing the harness onto your cluster with end user experience intact while adopting Kubernetes primitives for sandboxed execution, checkpoint/restore, scale, and security. Containers made this exact trip from developer machines to shared infrastructure in Kubernetes. In this keynote we\u0026#039;ll present harnessed agents as your cluster\u0026#039;s next critical workload. We\u0026#039;ll show how harnesses combine models with a modular runtime of tools, skills, and plugins, and how leading CNCF ecosystem projects deliver the identity, policy, and observability to run them in production.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T10:12:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T10:17:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["42ca2e0f-ba6c-4092-81a0-73eeca098181","cd0fdc7b-d298-48e8-b70d-c3f8a4c29c6b"]},{"id":"1301749","title":"Sandbox Your Agents","description":"\u003Cp\u003EAI Agents offer unequalled automation tooling for rapid software development, but with unfettered power comes great headaches, namely how to scope and secure them in cloud native stacks. A problematic agent with too much access, either through choice or a lack of knowledge, can take down entire production stacks and wipe databases. In this talk, we explore how using core community building blocks like Confidential Containers and OpenShell, alongside emerging technology across the cloud native ecosystem, allows anyone to isolate their agentic workloads and software development processes at scale with secure, containerized sandboxes.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T10:19:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T10:24:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["c84ee9c8-4982-4f94-8056-99b0737adafd"]},{"id":"1309267","title":"The Identity Crisis: Who is the AI Agent in Your Cluster?","description":"\u003Cp\u003EKubernetes was designed for a predictable world. We built it to manage deterministic, stateless microservices with known communication paths, defined resource requirements, and static identity boundaries.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThe rise of agentic AI completely shatters these assumptions.\u003Cbr\u003EAn AI agent is not just another stateless workload, it is a non-deterministic entity that generates dynamic network calls, triggers external APIs, and executes machine-generated code on the fly. This behavior introduces a security blind spot: when an autonomous agent invokes a local tool or accesses a cloud database, what identity does it present?\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EIn this keynote, Abdel Sghiouar unpacks the looming identity and resource crisis of running agents on Kubernetes. He will explore why traditional Authn/Authz and container boundaries fail when software behaves unpredictably, and showcase how emerging open-source standards are trying to redefine multi-tenancy and secure execution for the next decade of cloud-native computing.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T10:26:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T10:36:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["f2e1dff5-e8b9-4b4b-a8e4-4f5c6c61158f"]},{"id":"1227395","title":"Why We Bet the Data Platform on Kubernetes - And How AI Is Changing How We Operate It","description":"\u003Cp\u003EKubernetes has quietly become the default substrate for petabyte-scale data processing. Salesforce, Pinterest, Airbnb, and Apple all run native Spark, Flink, Trino, StarRocks, and Iceberg on Kubernetes at a scale the platform was never designed for.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThis panel of end-user operators talks about two things data leaders keep asking about. First, what does it actually take to run large-scale data on Kubernetes? Shuffle bottlenecks and Apache Celeborn, stateful upgrades, multi-tenant scheduling with YuniKorn and Kueue, Iceberg storage layouts, mixed CPU and GPU. Each panelist shares what broke at scale and how they fixed it.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003ESecond, how are AI agents changing day-2 operations? Troubleshooting agents for Spark and Flink, MCP servers for Spark History Server, agentic upgrade planning, autonomous tuning, AI-driven governance and lineage. Standard Kubernetes RBAC cannot govern non-deterministic actions driven by unvalidated prompts. This session presents a cloud-native architecture that integrates the Envoy AI Gateway with Kyverno\u2019s declarative policy model to govern autonomous AI intent before execution. The session demonstrates how Envoy acts as a specialized data plane for LLM traffic, using Envoy\u2019s External Processing API to \u0026quot;de-frame\u0026quot; Model Context Protocol (MCP) payloads. The Kyverno service then intercepts these extracted intents, applying declarative, YAML-based policies to authorize or block model actions in real time. In the last 18 months, those differences have been starkly emphasized. For over a decade K8s has been the industry standard platform for workloads of all sorts, with a rich ecosystem that has successfully adapted to every new class of workload. It\u2019s time to adapt again.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThe Agent Substrate (\u003Ca href=\u0022http://ate.dev\u0022 target=\u0022_blank\u0022 rel=\u0022noopener noreferrer\u0022\u003Ehttp://ate.dev\u003C/a\u003E) project was born to tackle the problem of agent-like workloads head-on.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003ELaunched in May, Agent Substrate\u2019s primary goal is to make it easy and efficient to run agent-like workloads. But an agent session is long-lived, stateful, bursty, and mostly idle.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EAnd it can do anything a user can. That\u0026#039;s what makes sandboxing critical.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThe sandbox defines what the agent can see, touch, call, and persist: filesystem access, tool permissions, credentials, network policy, identity, and cleanup. Getting that boundary wrong is a security incident waiting to happen.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThis talk covers the lessons we learned designing and implementing agent sandboxing for kagent - including NVIDIA\u0026#039;s OpenShell,  Kubernetes\u0026#039; agent-sandbox, and Google\u0026#039;s substrate support - and what teams need to think about before trusting agents with code execution, credentials, network access, and production data.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T17:30:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T18:00:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["4c68d4f9-2037-4d99-94ec-dcf2489d6dd2","f081932d-0f6b-4851-94bc-2eae3b2aad5b","1a06ab21-9ad3-4eeb-877c-9249ea11e645"]},{"id":"1250559","title":"GitOps Meltdown: How a Commit Triggered a Cascading Delete of 39 Clusters in Production","description":"\u003Cp\u003EGitOps assumes cluster state converges to Git.But, what happens when the desired state is wrong?\u003Cbr\u003EThis session examines a real incident where a routine Flux reconciliation turned a small git change into a cascading prune across a Kubernetes management platform managing 39 workload clusters. A missing Kustomization triggered inventory deletion, causing Flux controller to delete itself during reconciliation. Resulting in orphaned resources, stuck finalizers, and loss of critical Git repository storage.\u003Cbr\u003EUsing timelines and incident evidence, we trace the failure chain and explore Flux inventory tracking, pruning, finalizers, StatefulSet PVC ownership, CSI reclaim policies, and deletion ordering.\u003Cbr\u003EWe also cover recovery, restoring resources, rebuilding the GitOps control plane, and safely resuming reconciliation. Attendees will learn practical ways to reduce GitOps blast radius, protect stateful infrastructure, and build platforms that remain recoverable when automation fails.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-10T17:30:00","endsAt":"2026-11-10T18:00:00","roomId":82953,"speakers":["53ef16b1-4ebe-4505-b58e-7f4784eb2afd"]},{"id":"1294702","title":"The Flywheel Effect: Why Community Is the Ultimate End-User Advantage","description":"\u003Cp\u003ECloud native promises a future without limits, but every end-user organization eventually discovers the same truth: no team becomes limitless alone.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EEvery day, end users push CNCF projects into new industries, at new scales, and with entirely new challenges. The answer is infrastructure that runs autonomously, and that depends on real-time context: knowing how each workload behaves, what it needs, and what it talks to before any action is taken.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EYodar Shafrir shows how context, from a single workload to the whole system, becomes autonomous orchestration that keeps enterprise AI reliable and performant, and puts platform teams in command of the system instead of chasing it.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-11T09:50:00","endsAt":"2026-11-11T09:55:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["334213b5-8d7b-48dc-90e0-9a1e8cf5ce7b"]},{"id":"1360829","title":"We Have GitOps at Home: How Meta Went from Terraform on Cron to GitOps for AI Infra","description":"\u003Cp\u003EAt Meta, ~15 engineers run ~100 Kubernetes clusters for AI research \u0026amp; inference. Then AI arrived. Inference, the most sensitive layer in the stack, became a call to a vendor API. Your cluster is sovereign. Your AI isn\u0026#039;t.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EYou already run what\u0026#039;s needed to reclaim that layer. An inference request is plain HTTP, with the model name in the JSON body. The ingress and Gateway API patterns in the cluster today can route and balance that traffic, and apply policy at the boundary. One data plane, instead of a fragmented traffic stack.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThis session covers consistent-hashing across GPU backends and model-aware routing from request inspection, with inference staying inside the cluster. Everything runs on HAProxy, the open source, model-agnostic load balancer and ingress controller built for high throughput and low latency. But we also knew that achieving our goal would require software we\u2019d have to build: a meta control plane that could weave these projects together into a single streamlined platform. We call the platform CAP and we\u2019re excited to share its design, show a brief demo, and talk about our transition from end user to open source maintainer and contributor as CAP evolves from an internal platform to a brand new open source project.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-11T10:23:00","endsAt":"2026-11-11T10:28:00","roomId":82947,"speakers":["54570209-5ec9-4392-9680-38679ee15e97","5b142ce7-0b58-425c-84ab-999c42a83605"]},{"id":"1345967","title":"KubeRay 101","description":"\u003Cp\u003EKubeRay is the Kubernetes-native operator for running Ray workloads, providing lifecycle management for Ray clusters, jobs, and production services on Kubernetes.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThis Birds of a Feather session is an introduction to KubeRay led by members of the KubeRay Technical Steering Committee. AI agents can generate plausible SQL while misunderstanding business metrics, choosing incorrect joins, or bypassing governance rules. Semantic Operator addresses this by running Apache Ossie semantic models as Kubernetes resources. It provides agents and applications with certified metrics and dimensions, then generates deterministic, governed SQL for StarRocks or Trino. In this live demo, we will show how to manage semantic models through a Kubernetes operator, validate schemas and detect physical drift, enforce row, column, and metric governance, plan deterministic queries, and expose MCP and REST access for AI agents and applications. We will also walk through the end to end architecture and potential integration points.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-11T13:58:00","endsAt":"2026-11-11T14:03:00","roomId":90363,"speakers":["00407ab5-f8e4-4d04-b154-551208836c96"]},{"id":"1333711","title":"End-User Panel \u2013 KubeFlow Enterprise Use Cases-Solutions","description":"\u003Cp\u003EPanelists will discuss how their organizations leverage Kubeflow to orchestrate AI workloads on Kubernetes\u2014from distributed training to low-latency serving\u2014while overcoming enterprise challenges such as scalability, pipeline automation and hybrid-cloud integration. In this session, Lucy Sweet (Member of Technical Staff at Anthropic and Node Lifecycle WG co-Lead for the Kubernetes project) and Sandeep Kanabar (Lead Software Engineer at Gen) will take you on a live journey through setting up Kubernetes \u201cThe Hard Way\u201d. To compensate, the ecosystem evolved many external schedulers, including Kueue, Volcano, and KAI, each forcing controllers to pick a side.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EKubernetes 1.36 changes this. The new Workload and PodGroup APIs (KEP-4671) introduce scheduler-native primitives for gang-scheduling, topology-aware placement, and coordinated use of high-bandwidth interconnects such as IMEX. TrainJob, JobSet, and LeaderWorkerSet are converging on these APIs.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EThis session covers Kubeflow Trainer\u2019s adoption (KEP-3015): why TrainJob owns Workload composition and how its plugin architecture enables advanced scheduling features. Attendees will see a demo of multi-node fine-tuning on modern accelerators, how the Workload API unifies a fragmented ecosystem, and how to adopt it in their own controllers.\u003C/p\u003E","startsAt":"2026-11-11T17:00:00","endsAt":"2026-11-11T17:30:00","roomId":82948,"speakers":["d2462872-1ca2-4a95-a111-2ec722768036"]},{"id":"1289660","title":"The Future of Kubernetes Eviction and Node Lifecycle","description":"\u003Cp\u003EKubernetes disruption handling is evolving from a collection of custom solutions and workarounds into a more cooperative lifecycle model. Join the Node Lifecycle Working Group for an update on two key efforts: the Eviction Request API for workload disruption coordination, and Specialized Lifecycle Management.\u003C/p\u003E\u003Cp\u003EWe will discuss how the new declarative Eviction API gives workloads, controllers, and administrators a more explicit way to negotiate disruption than today\u2019s best-effort eviction paths.
